clue.text: Hit fine pull shot over Crawley's head (poor delivery)

indicators.note: Something described as shot is wrecked and past holding its shape, so these letters will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: three letters of fodder, taken straight off the clue
F is fine on a pencil, and the crossword's usual short form for the word
four more letters, the cricket stroke lending its name to the fodder
Zak Crawley opens the batting for England, and a name's head is the letter it starts with

explanation.surface: A batter middles a pull shot and the ball sails over a fielder's head.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket vocabulary works both sides of the clue: 'shot' looks like the stroke being described and is really the shuffle instruction, while the definition sits quietly in the brackets.
explanation.definitionFit: A full pitch reaches the batter without bouncing, which is a gift to hit and so a bowler's bad ball.

clue.text: Unable to outrun wolves, must one turn to this beauty treatment?

parts.note: to face something is to turn and meet it head on
wolves run in a pack, and outrunning one is not on offer

explanation.surface: Someone caught in the open with wolves closing in and no chance of outrunning them.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark carries the whole joke: the clue never claims the phrase is a beauty treatment, it asks whether the words the wolves force on you happen to name one.
explanation.definitionFit: A face pack is the gloop you spread on and leave to set, sold as a treatment for the look of the skin.

clue.text: Antagonist of Bond film topped by M's predecessor

indicators.note: In a down entry the topping piece sits above the rest, so this letter goes on the front.

parts.note: the letter that comes before M in the alphabet
Ben Affleck's 2012 Tehran thriller, four letters of title

explanation.surface: A rundown of a Bond film's cast, the villain listed under whoever ran the service before M.
explanation.walkthrough: 'M's predecessor' looks like spy history — whoever had the job before M — and it is only the letter standing before M in the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Emilio Largo is the eyepatched villain of Thunderball, so the name defines an enemy of 007 by example.

clue.text: Man's lover arranged NHS hospital trip to discharge son

indicators.note: Arranging a trip means settling what order things come in, and here a new order is settled for the letters.
Discharging a patient sends them out of the hospital, and this sends one letter out of the fodder.

parts.note: fifteen letters offered up, one more than the grid has room for
S is the standard short form for son, and it is the letter sent out

explanation.surface: A partner fixes up a hospital visit so that a son can be sent home.
explanation.walkthrough: The NHS is Britain's health service, and 'discharge' does the setter's work twice: hospital word on the surface, deletion instruction underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Philanthropy is love of mankind, from the Greek philos and anthropos, so the word names someone who loves Man in the collective.

clue.text: Jewel merchant and his glassmaker son, did they quarrel at all?

definitions.text: Jewel merchant and his glassmaker son

parts.note: a tiff is a small quarrel, the kind that blows over by teatime
'did they eat at all' and 'did they eat any' ask the same question

explanation.surface: A father-and-son business in jewels and glass, and the question of whether the two ever fell out.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark at the end is the tell that the last four words are wordplay rather than biography: nothing is being claimed about a family row.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lewis Tiffany founded the New York jewellers and his son Louis Comfort made the stained glass, so one surname covers both men.

clue.text: Hamlet's intimate means to compare Santa Clauses?

parts.note: Santa's laugh is ho ho ho, so HO is the syllable he is made of
a ratio is how you set two quantities against each other

explanation.surface: Somebody wondering how you would measure one Father Christmas against another.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer after two letters and it becomes a unit of measurement for Father Christmases, which is what the question mark is apologising for.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio is the friend Hamlet trusts with everything and the one left alive to tell the story, so intimate means closest confidant.

clue.text: What follows wine, women … turned on … ?

definitions.text: What follows wine, women … turned on … ?

indicators.note: the word named next is turned round where it sits inside the other word

parts.note: the saying is 'wine, women and song', so song comes after those two
the clue's own word, taken as written

explanation.surface: After the drink and company, aroused, what comes next?
explanation.walkthrough: Complete the saying 'wine, women and song', then 'turned' reverses the ON inside SONG to NO. Read whole, the clue also says what happens once people are turned on after wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A snog is British slang for a long passionate kiss, the natural next step for an aroused couple.

clue.text: Like some leaves I needn't've braised

indicators.note: Braising breaks a thing down in the pot until it no longer holds its original shape, and these letters go the same way.

parts.note: nine letters once the apostrophes are dropped, exactly what the grid needs

explanation.surface: A cook regretting the leaves they put in the pan.
explanation.walkthrough: The contraction is the whole difficulty: 'needn't've' is barely written English, which is why what it hands over does not look like fodder at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Net-veined describes a leaf whose veins branch into a network instead of running in parallel, which is how most broadleaf leaves look.

clue.text: One in a special class

indicators.note: The small word is doing positional work: what is 'in' something sits inside its letters.

parts.note: a genus is the rank a biologist sorts creatures into, one step above species
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A pupil taken out of the ordinary form and put into a class of their own.
explanation.walkthrough: Taxonomy is both trap and key: 'class' is a rank in the same system as genus, so the clue points at the wrong rung of that ladder on purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone of genius is in a class of their own, which is what the clue says straight: one person, and a class kept for them.

clue.text: Faith right to stop Cross and Cook climbing peak of Mount Sinai

indicators.note: the letter plugs a gap in the run of pieces, as a stopper does

parts.note: a zo (also dzo or zho) is a cross between a yak and a cow
to roast is to cook

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means read upwards, so these letters are reversed
the peak is the top, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: its first letter is used
taken as written

explanation.surface: A religion, with references to the cross, cooking and the mountain where Moses received the law.
explanation.walkthrough: A zo is a yak-cow hybrid, a crossword favourite. 'peak of' Mount is M; 'climbing' reverses M plus SINAI to IANISM, and 'to stop' puts R between ROAST and that.
explanation.definitionFit: Zoroastrianism is the ancient Persian religion founded by Zoroaster, still practised by the Parsis, so it is a faith.

clue.text: Old queen's favourite brother, Joe

parts.note: 'oh brother!' and 'cor!' are the same noise of surprise, one British and dated
GI Joe is the American soldier, and GI is the crossword's standard one

explanation.surface: Gossip about an old queen's favourite, and about the brother, Joe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old queen' is the late Elizabeth II, whose dogs were a national fixture, while the wordplay needs 'brother' heard as an exclamation rather than a relative.
explanation.definitionFit: The late Queen Elizabeth kept these short-legged Welsh dogs all her life, so the breed is named by its most famous owner.

clue.text: Neglected wetland in which ordinary river has become dry

indicators.note: Whatever the clue says is in the wetland goes bodily inside that word's letters.

parts.note: a fen is the flat marshy ground of eastern England
O is the standard short form for ordinary
R is the standard short form for river, as on a map
milk goes sour and bread goes stale: to go a thing is to become it
TT is teetotal, the crossword's usual dry

explanation.surface: A marsh that has dried out, its ordinary little river gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' as teetotal and 'go' as become are the two everyday senses hiding behind the drought, and neither announces itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing forgotten has slipped out of mind and so gets no attention, which is exactly the complaint in calling it neglected.

clue.text: Commensurately paid singer left for auditorium

parts.note: a pro is the paid one, as against the amateur

indicators.note: An auditorium is a room built for hearing, so what counts is the sound of the word rather than its spelling.

parts.note: a rat is both the one who sings to the police and the one who deserts, so someone who has done it is a ratter

explanation.surface: A singer on proper wages setting off for the concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' is the crook's word here — the one who has informed on everybody else — and the auditorium is asking for the sound of that person, not the spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro rata is the Latin for in proportion, so a wage worked out pro rata is set commensurately with the hours or the share.

clue.text: Formally, you are, curiously, probing social critic

indicators.note: Curiously means oddly, and letters described as odd are letters no longer in their proper order.

parts.note: 'thou' is the archaic you that now sounds formal, with 'are' following it unchanged

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned way of saying you are, dropped into a remark about a critic of society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Probing' looks like an insertion instruction and belongs to the definition, while the fodder hides in plain sight as a Sunday-best version of 'you are'.
explanation.definitionFit: Walden and Civil Disobedience put American society under the microscope, so Thoreau is a social critic and a searching one.

clue.text: To acquire Amtrak, possibly involve US clodhopper

indicators.note: 'Possibly' warns that the name is only an example, so what the wordplay wants is the general kind of outfit it belongs to.

parts.note: to involve someone is to count them in, and the phrase splits apart around what follows
America's passenger rail operator: RY for railway, CO for company
the two letters stand exactly as written

explanation.surface: Buying Amtrak would probably mean bringing the American government in on the deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Amtrak is the United States' national passenger railway, and 'possibly' is the warning that the letters wanted are the generic operator rather than the name itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A country cousin is the unpolished relative up from the sticks, which is what calling somebody a clodhopper says: clumsy and rustic.

clue.text: Who's reprimanding United attacker for preserving lead?

indicators.note: To preserve a thing is to keep hold of it, and what is kept is held inside rather than tacked on the end.

parts.note: U is how football's United is written on a fixture list
a raider attacks and gets out again, which covers the soldier and the forward alike
Pb is lead's chemical symbol, from the Latin plumbum

explanation.surface: A manager tearing into a United forward who is only trying to protect a one-goal lead.
explanation.walkthrough: Football and chemistry collide on one word: 'lead' looks like the scoreline the attacker is guarding and is the metal's symbol instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To upbraid is to tell someone off at length, so the person doing the reprimanding is an upbraider.

clue.text: Mr Pearce unwisely let a lot of folk use his dominant partner

definitions.text: Mr Pearce unwisely let a lot of folk use his
definitions.meaning: the Devon folk song Widecombe Fair begins 'Tom Pearce, Tom Pearce, lend me your...', and seven men then ride the borrowed animal to death
Chambers files this sense under the second word: the proverbial wife who is the better horse of the pair

explanation.surface: A man who foolishly let half the village borrow the one who really rules him.
explanation.walkthrough: Two pieces of very English general knowledge meet on one phrase: a Dartmoor folk song about a lent-out horse, and the old proverb about which half of a marriage is in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says the grey mare is the better horse, meaning the wife rules the house; in the song she is the animal Tom Pearce lends out.

clue.text: Barrels were returned empty? I'm not sure I can forgo tack

definitions.note: The definition is written in the answer's own voice: 'I' is the person the answer names, and the rest of the clause is what makes them that person rather than any other.

parts.note: an empty shelf is a bare one
goods returned have come back
a rider is the reservation attached to an agreement, which is what stopping short of sure adds

explanation.surface: A carter checking whether the barrels came back empty, and doubting he can manage without his gear.
explanation.walkthrough: A horse's barrel is the part of its body the saddle sits on, which is why the first half reads as trade talk while the answer is equestrian.
explanation.definitionFit: Tack is the saddle and bridle a horse is fitted out with, and doing without it is exactly what this rider is named for.

clue.text: Performers in show withdrawing favourite number

indicators.note: A thing withdrawing pulls back the way it came, so these letters are read in the opposite direction.

parts.note: the bill is the printed list of who is on, so it stands in for the performers
the favourite is the No 1, and No with the Roman one drawn back gives these three

explanation.surface: A theatre pulling its star turn out of the programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No 1' is the favourite written as a racecard writes it, Roman numeral and all, and it is that scrap of shorthand that turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: A billion is a number in the plainest sense, a thousand million: the figure itself rather than a quantity of anything.

clue.text: Turner makes function appear larger on screen?

parts.note: typing in caps is how letters are made to look bigger on a screen
tan is a trigonometric function, alongside sin and cos

explanation.surface: Somebody enlarging a function on a monitor so it can be read from further off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turner' wants to be the painter and is a piece of deck machinery instead, while the rest of the clue is a maths function shouted in capitals.
explanation.definitionFit: A capstan is the upright drum a crew walks round to wind in a cable, so it is a turner in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Wanting a taste of 25, cook basmati dish

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter is missing from the rice before it is rearranged
to cook something is to work it into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the rice's letters are the fodder

indicators.note: a taste is only a small first bit, so the first letter is taken

parts.note: the answer to 25 across, INDIA

explanation.surface: Without a hint of Indian spice, prepare a rice dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a taste of 25' is I, the first letter of INDIA (25 across). 'Wanting' takes it out of BASMATI, and 'cook' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Tsamba is a Tibetan staple of roasted barley flour, so it is a dish of food.

clue.text: Essential for operator training to cut speaker's initial connection

indicators.note: Cutting into a word opens a gap in the middle of it, and that gap is where the next piece lands.

parts.note: the initial of speaker is the letter it begins with
a call is the connection you make down a telephone line
PE is the school timetable's physical training

explanation.surface: A trainee switchboard operator cutting off the first caller of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operator' is a switchboard on the surface and a surgeon underneath, and 'cut' belongs to neither: it is the instruction that opens the telephone word up.
explanation.definitionFit: The operator here is a surgeon, and the scalpel is the blade they cannot open a patient without.

clue.text: Libertine tactic used to find car park space for Spooner?

indicators.note: Spooner, the Oxford don famed for swapping word beginnings, signals an exchange of the two words' opening sounds

parts.note: a bay is a marked parking space
a ploy is a cunning tactic; Spooner swaps sounds, not spellings, so it is the spoken 'ploi' whose vowel sound goes to make 'boy'

explanation.surface: A womaniser's trick for getting a parking spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for Spooner' asks for the opening sounds swapped: a BAY PLOY (a tactic to find a parking bay) said with B and PL exchanged comes out as PLAY BOY.
explanation.definitionFit: A playboy is a wealthy man devoted to pleasure and affairs, so he is a libertine.

clue.text: Bathroom 'fixture'? It'd be 'fitting'

indicators.note: A bathroom fitting is a thing plumbed in, but fitting also means apt, and letters made to fit are letters rearranged.

parts.note: five letters once the apostrophe is dropped, which is all the grid asks for

explanation.surface: Someone joking that a certain bathroom fixture would be just the right thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Both quoted words do sly duty: 'fixture' is plumbing vocabulary borrowed for the definition, and 'fitting' is the plumber's noun used as a shuffle instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A bidet is plumbed in beside the loo, so it counts as a bathroom fixture — the quotation marks admit the setter is winking at the word.

clue.text: On counter, neatly sews single storage unit in garment

indicators.note: To run counter to something is to run against it, so this piece is written the other way round.

parts.note: to trim a garment is to sew edging neatly onto it, and those four letters run backwards here

indicators.note: What the clue puts 'in' the other word goes bodily inside its letters.

parts.note: I is one, the Roman numeral
a disk is where a computer keeps its files

explanation.surface: A tailor at the shop counter, sewing neatly and fitting a storage unit into a piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Almost everything reads as tailoring — the counter, the neat sewing, the garment — and the storage unit belongs to another century entirely, which is what gives the game away.
explanation.definitionFit: A midi skirt is the calf-length one, sitting between mini and maxi, and a skirt is a garment.

clue.text: International relief supplies finally flown around land

indicators.note: 'Finally' asks for the end of the word it sits beside, which comes to a single letter.

parts.note: I is the standard short form for international

indicators.note: Something sent around comes back the other way about, so those letters are read in reverse.

parts.note: the last letter of flown, as asked for
relief supplies are aid, and the word is turned about

explanation.surface: Emergency aid flown out to a disaster and dropped over the country that needed it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally flown' is the smallest piece here and the easiest to skate past: it is one letter, the last of the word standing next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a country, and 'land' is the loose old word for one: a nation thought of as its territory.

clue.text: Which current runs through area by centre of Leeds?

definitions.text: Which current runs through area by centre of Leeds?

indicators.note: A thing that runs through something else passes inside it, so this letter is planted in the middle.

parts.note: an are is the metric unit of area, a hundred square metres
I is the physicist's symbol for electrical current

explanation.surface: A quiz question about which river flows through the middle of Leeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds stands on this river, so the sentence is a straight question as well as a set of instructions; 'area' wants the metric unit, not the general word.
explanation.definitionFit: The river through Leeds is the one wanted, and 'current' is fair for it, a river being a body of water in constant flow.

clue.text: Small unit moving near to Bury not including this person

indicators.note: the rearranged letters bury, so surround, the next piece
moving the letters around rearranges them

parts.note: its letters are the fodder

indicators.note: the word wraps round the next piece

parts.note: taken as written
me is the setter speaking of themselves

explanation.surface: A little army unit relocating close to the town of Bury, without me.
explanation.walkthrough: A nest of containers: 'moving' rearranges NEAR to NARE, and 'to Bury' puts inside it NOT 'including' ME. Bury is a town near Manchester, so it looks like a place.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre, a tiny measure of length.
